lines.t: In old libraries, every book sat on the shelf backwards. Spine to the wall. And nobody thought that was strange.
Because back then, one book could cost as much as a house. Every page was copied by hand.
And thieves knew it. Even hungry students would slip a book under their coat and sell it.
So the librarians came up with a plan. A chain. On every valuable book.
But a chain on the spine would rip the binding apart. So they bolted it to the front edge of the cover.
And if the chain hangs from the front... the book has to face the wrong way round.
You see, it's like a dog on a leash. The leash goes where the dog's face is, not its tail.
So you'd pull the book down, open it right there on a desk, and read it still on its chain.
Want to take it home? Only the librarian had the key.
Then printing made books cheap, and the chains slowly came off.
But one cathedral in England still keeps about fifteen hundred books on their chains. The biggest chained library left.
And one library in Dublin had a different idea. They didn't chain the books...
they locked the readers in cages.
Your library, your rules. A, chain the books. Or B, cage the readers.
